map.string: Reflections of changes nearby catch up a little later
Reflection probes that are already complete refresh one cube face every few frames instead of every frame. New probes still update at once.
Moving avatars and objects show in reflections with a delay
Reflection detail goes from Real-time to Static and dynamic: the probe around the camera is no longer redrawn every frame.
Real-time reflections update a little less smoothly
The real-time reflection probe renders two cube faces a frame instead of the whole cube, so a full update is spread over three frames.
Distant scenery drops out of reflections
Reflection probes draw the scene only to half the distance. Each probe update draws less, which matters most in built-up places.
Objects lose their automatic reflection probes; placed probes, terrain and water keep theirs
Reflection coverage goes from "manual, terrain, water and objects" to "manual, terrain and water", so there are fewer probes to update.
Fewer local reflections in busy places
Halves the number of reflection probes kept. Fewer probes are updated and searched for each pixel of the lighting pass.
Reflections slightly softer on fine normal-map detail
Screen-space reflections are traced at half resolution and read back filtered.
Reflections of far things may be missed
Halves the most steps a screen-space reflection ray may take through the depth pyramid.
Floors and water stop reflecting nearby avatars and objects; probe reflections remain
Turns screen-space reflections off. Reflections come from the reflection probes only.
Slightly softer ambient occlusion in corners
Ground-truth ambient occlusion is computed at half resolution and filtered back up: roughly a quarter of its cost.
One slice direction less per pixel for ground-truth ambient occlusion. Rebuilds the shaders.
Ambient occlusion goes back to the classic, flatter SSAO
Turns ground-truth ambient occlusion off; the classic screen-space ambient occlusion is used instead.
Light cones a little softer at their edges
The volumetric projector light is marched at half the resolution.
Fewer projectors show a light cone (the nearest keep theirs)
Halves the number of projectors that get a volumetric light cone.
Halves the samples taken along each view ray through a projector cone.
No light cones in the air from projectors
Turns the volumetric projector light off.
Halves the cells across the water ripple grid: about a quarter of the simulation work.
Water no longer reacts to avatars, boats and splashes
Turns interactive water ripples off: no simulation, and the water shaders go back to the plain surface. Rebuilds the shaders.
Distant shadows of moving things follow a frame late
The two far sun shadow maps are redrawn every other frame. Moving or turning the camera, or the sun moving, still redraws them at once.
The two far sun shadow maps are drawn at half the resolution of the near ones.
Keeps the shadows of static objects and terrain in the far sun shadow maps in a cache; only moving, rigged and alpha-masked things are redrawn each update.
Keeps the shadows of static objects and terrain in the far sun shadow maps in a cache, so far fewer objects are sorted and drawn into them each update.
Shadow maps are drawn at three quarters of their resolution.
Things moving in projector light cast their shadow a frame late
Projector shadows whose light and settings are unchanged are redrawn every other frame.
Shadow edges a little less smooth
Halves the samples of the shadow and ambient occlusion blur.
No sun shadows beyond the shorter distance; nearer shadows get sharper
Sun and moon shadows reach half as far, so fewer objects are culled and sorted for the shadow maps.
Shadows of moving avatars near lights lag a little
Local light shadow maps redraw half as many cube faces a frame. Faces whose casters moved wait their turn, so their culling, sorting and drawing is spread over more frames.
Shadows of moving avatars near lights lag a little
Local light shadow maps redraw half as many cube faces a frame. Faces whose casters moved wait their turn, so their culling, sorting and drawing is spread over more frames.
Fewer local lights cast shadows; the others shine through walls again
Halves the number of local point lights with a shadow map. The lights that matter most on screen keep theirs; each one dropped saves six faces to cull and draw.
Fewer local lights cast shadows; the others shine through walls again
Halves the number of local point lights with a shadow map. The lights that matter most on screen keep theirs; each one dropped saves six faces to cull and draw.
Local light shadow edges a little softer
Local light shadow map faces go to 1024 texels across: each face redrawn fills a quarter of the texels, and the maps take a quarter of the memory (48 MB a light instead of 192 MB).
Local light shadow edges a little softer
Local light shadow map faces go to 1024 texels across: each face redrawn fills a quarter of the texels, and the maps take a quarter of the memory (48 MB a light instead of 192 MB).
Avatars far from a light cast no shadow from it
Other avatars more than 6 m from a local light cast no shadow into its maps; yours always does. In a crowd the avatars are most of what the local light shadows draw.
Avatars far from a light cast no shadow from it
Other avatars more than 6 m from a local light cast no shadow into its maps; yours always does. In a crowd the avatars are most of what the local light shadows draw.
Avatar shadows from local lights may change shape as the camera moves away
Rigged meshes near a light with a shadow map no longer keep the detail seen from the light, so distant avatars near lights are drawn with fewer triangles.
Distant avatars cast no sun shadow
Other avatars and animesh cast into the two nearest sun shadow maps only. The far maps stop drawing every rigged mesh again for shadows a few texels across. Your own avatar always casts.
Distant avatars cast no sun shadow
Other avatars and animesh cast into the two nearest sun shadow maps only. The far maps stop drawing every rigged mesh again for shadows a few texels across. Your own avatar always casts.
Avatars past 48 m cast no shadow
Avatars and animesh more than 48 m from the camera, with their attachments, cast no shadow. Your own avatar always casts.
Avatars past 48 m cast no shadow
Avatars and animesh more than 48 m from the camera, with their attachments, cast no shadow. Your own avatar always casts.
Distant leaves, grass and fences cast plain or no sun shadow
Only the two nearest sun shadow maps draw alpha tested casters (leaves, grass, fences). In the far maps their shadows are a few texels across and cost a large share of the shadow pass.
Distant leaves, grass and fences cast plain or no sun shadow
Only the two nearest sun shadow maps draw alpha tested casters (leaves, grass, fences). In the far maps their shadows are a few texels across and cost a large share of the shadow pass.
Sun shadows take 3 lookups instead of 5 where an area is clearly fully lit or fully shadowed, and all 5 only near shadow edges.
Shadows lose their soft edges that widen away from the caster
Soft shadows (PCSS) off: the sun and projector shadows are filtered with the plain kernel instead of the blocker search and the wide filter.
Sunlight through stained or tinted glass is no longer coloured
Coloured sun shadows off: the two nearest sun shadow maps no longer draw the alpha blended objects again into a colour map.
Alpha blended objects cast no shadow
Alpha blended objects (glass, animated transparent effects) are no longer drawn into the shadow maps.
The glow map is half the width and height.
No bloom around bright parts (the classic glow stays)
Edges a little softer, fine detail slightly blurred
Antialiasing goes from SMAA to FXAA, a single cheaper pass.
Smoke and fog particles lit more simply
Particles are lit by the sky probe and one shadow sample instead of the full lighting.
Halves the most particles kept at once, so fewer are simulated each frame.
Hair and sheer clothing of avatars further away lit more simply
The blended transparent parts of avatars beyond the cheap avatar alpha distance are lit like cheap particles.
Simpler hair lighting starts closer to the camera
Halves the distance beyond which avatar transparent parts are lit cheaply.
Avatars past the nearest 12 drawn as impostors, animating less often
Limits fully drawn avatars to 12; the others become impostors, which are updated less often.
More distant avatars drawn as impostors
Lowers the number of fully drawn avatars by a third.
Very complex avatars shown as solid-colour shapes
Sets the avatar complexity limit to 250000. Avatars above it are drawn as plain shapes. You can still show any one of them fully from its context menu.
Draw distance three quarters as far. Culling and sorting handle fewer objects; most of their work is near you, so expect a modest saving.
Draw distance three quarters as far, so fewer objects are drawn. Distant objects cover few pixels, so expect a modest saving.
The 3D scene gets softer while the frame rate is low; the UI stays sharp
Lowers the scene resolution in steps when the frame rate is under its target, and raises it again when there is headroom.
Changing text and counters in windows update a little later
The 2D UI is drawn into its own buffer and redrawn only when needed (every frame while you use it), instead of every frame.
Changing text and counters in windows update a little later
The 2D UI is drawn into its own buffer and redrawn only when needed (every frame while you use it), instead of every frame.
None; hidden objects are culled the classic way
Turns GPU occlusion culling off. Its second phase was costly here (seen on AMD cards), more than it saves.
No bounced light from nearby surfaces
No soft ambient shadow around avatars
Turns the soft occlusion around avatars off, which the full-screen lighting pass computes for every pixel.
Local point lights are shaded in one full screen pass, each pixel lit only by the lights of its own screen tile, instead of one light volume draw per light.
Local point lights are shaded in one full screen pass, each pixel lit only by the lights of its own screen tile, instead of one light volume draw per light.
Fewer local lights glow in the air
Halves the number of point lights whose light glows in the air; the ones that weigh most on screen keep it.
No glow in the air around local lights
The glow of local point lights in the air is no longer drawn.
Ambient light leaks a little more into creases and corners
Bent normals off: the half resolution pass that finds the most open direction of each point no longer runs.
Inside corners, creases and seams less dark
Crease occlusion off: about 20 fewer depth reads per pixel in the sun light pass.
Avatar skin loses its soft light bleed past shadow edges
Skin subsurface scattering off: the screen-space pass that diffuses the light on avatar skin no longer runs.
Halves the samples along each sun ray.
Sun rays are computed at half the screen resolution.
No sun ray shafts in the air
Sun rays off: the light scattered in the air is no longer ray marched.
Halves the samples along each view ray for the underwater light rays.
No dust specks in sun rays and projector light
Dust motes off: the drifting specks in lit air are no longer drawn.
Rigged alpha faces that can never fail the alpha test are drawn without it, so the graphics card can skip the hidden hair and clothing layers behind them early.
Some rigged faces lose their soft alpha fringe
Rigged faces whose alpha is all on or off are drawn as cutouts with the opaque surfaces instead of blended in the alpha pass. Rebuilds every object once.
In a crowd, nearby hair and sheer clothing lit more simply
With 8 or more avatars drawn in full, the transparent parts of every other avatar are lit cheaply, whatever their distance.
Avatars that cover less than 2 percent of the view have their transparent parts lit cheaply, whatever their distance.
The heaviest bodies, hair and clothing of nearby avatars show less detail
Each other avatar gets about 300000 triangles: while over, its heaviest rigged mesh drops one level of detail.
Inner hair layers may draw over outer ones again
Rigged alpha mesh is drawn in one pass instead of a solid core, a blended fringe and a depth pass.
Rough surfaces show probe reflections instead of screen-space ones
Screen-space reflections are traced only on surfaces smoother than 0.6 roughness; rougher ones, where the reflection is a blur anyway, keep the reflection probes.
Medium-rough reflections may show faint copies of bright objects
Reflection probes are prefiltered with the stock number of samples.
Flat, low contrast areas very slightly softer
NVIDIA RTX and GTX 16xx only: tiles of the opaque pass that were low in contrast, the sky and blurred areas shade once per few pixels. Edges stay at full rate.
Textures behind walls may load back in when they come into view
Textures of objects hidden behind others are allowed to drop detail first, so visible ones keep theirs while memory is short.
Draw distance three quarters as far: fewer objects, fewer textures to hold, so the ones near you stay sharp.
Texture detail was held down while video memory was still free. Halving the soft zone lets textures use more of it before detail is lowered.
Texture detail was held down while video memory was still free. Halving the soft zone lets textures use more of it before detail is lowered.
There is headroom: ground-truth ambient occlusion back at full resolution.
There is headroom: shadow maps drawn at a higher resolution.
Distant shadows of moving things follow at once
There is headroom: the far sun shadow maps redrawn every frame.
Reflections catch up with changes sooner
There is headroom: reflection probes refresh more often.
There is headroom: draw distance a quarter further.
There is headroom: particles lit by the nearby reflection probes and full shadows again.
There is headroom: screen-space reflections traced at full resolution.
Water reacts to avatars, boats and splashes
There is headroom: interactive water ripples on, with rings, wakes and splashes around avatars and moving objects in the water. About 0.1 to 0.2 ms of GPU time. Rebuilds the shaders.
There is headroom: four more avatars drawn fully instead of as impostors.
